claim: Primary sensory neurons are generally considered the only source of dorsal horn calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).
source: Primary sensory neurons are generally considered the only source of dorsal horn calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a neuropeptide critical to the transmission of pain messages.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific consensus in the abstract.

claim: CGRP is a neuropeptide critical to the transmission of pain messages.
source: Primary sensory neurons are generally considered the only source of dorsal horn calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a neuropeptide critical to the transmission of pain messages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A distinct population of CGRP-expressing excitatory interneurons exists in lamina III of the spinal cord dorsal horn and trigeminal nucleus caudalis.
source: Using a tamoxifen-inducible CalcaCreER transgenic mouse, here we identified a distinct population of CGRP-expressing excitatory interneurons in lamina III of the spinal cord dorsal horn and trigeminal nucleus caudalis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data from the transgenic mouse model.

claim: CGRP interneurons have spine-laden, dorsally directed dendrites.
source: These interneurons have spine-laden, dorsally directed, dendrites, and ventrally directed axons.
evidence: This morphological characterization is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data.

claim: CGRP interneurons have ventrally directed axons.
source: These interneurons have spine-laden, dorsally directed, dendrites, and ventrally directed axons.
evidence: This morphological characterization is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data.

claim: Under resting conditions, CGRP interneurons are under tonic inhibitory control.
source: As under resting conditions, CGRP interneurons are under tonic inhibitory control, neither innocuous nor noxious stimulation provoked significant Fos expression in these neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data showing effects of bicuculline and strychnine.

claim: Neither innocuous nor noxious stimulation provoked significant Fos expression in CGRP interneurons under resting conditions.
source: As under resting conditions, CGRP interneurons are under tonic inhibitory control, neither innocuous nor noxious stimulation provoked significant Fos expression in these neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Fos immunostaining data.

claim: Synchronous, electrical non-nociceptive Aβ primary afferent stimulation of dorsal roots depolarized the CGRP interneurons.
source: However, synchronous, electrical non-nociceptive Aβ primary afferent stimulation of dorsal roots depolarized the CGRP interneurons, consistent with their receipt of a VGLUT1 innervation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: CGRP interneurons receive VGLUT1 innervation.
source: However, synchronous, electrical non-nociceptive Aβ primary afferent stimulation of dorsal roots depolarized the CGRP interneurons, consistent with their receipt of a VGLUT1 innervation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemical data showing VGLUT1 appositions.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CGRP interneurons produced mechanical hypersensitivity in response to von Frey stimulation.
source: On the other hand, chemogenetic activation of the neurons produced a mechanical hypersensitivity in response to von Frey stimulation, whereas their caspase-mediated ablation led to mechanical hyposensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by DREADD activation experiments.

claim: Caspase-mediated ablation of CGRP interneurons led to mechanical hyposensitivity.
source: On the other hand, chemogenetic activation of the neurons produced a mechanical hypersensitivity in response to von Frey stimulation, whereas their caspase-mediated ablation led to mechanical hyposensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by ablation experiments.

claim: After partial peripheral nerve injury, innocuous stimulation (brush) induced significant Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons.
source: Finally, after partial peripheral nerve injury, innocuous stimulation (brush) induced significant Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Fos immunostaining data after SNI.

claim: CGRP interneurons become hyperexcitable after nerve injury.
source: These findings suggest that CGRP interneurons become hyperexcitable and contribute either to ascending circuits originating in deep dorsal horn or to the reflex circuits in baseline conditions, but not in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that brush stimulation activates CGRP interneurons only after nerve injury.

claim: CGRP interneurons contribute either to ascending circuits originating in deep dorsal horn or to the reflex circuits in baseline conditions.
source: These findings suggest that CGRP interneurons become hyperexcitable and contribute either to ascending circuits originating in deep dorsal horn or to the reflex circuits in baseline conditions, but not in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the abstract based on the anatomical and functional data.

claim: CGRP is the most prominent molecular marker of the peptidergic subpopulation of primary afferent nociceptors.
source: Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is the most prominent molecular marker of the peptidergic subpopulation of primary afferent nociceptors (Basbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: When released from peripheral terminals of sensory neurons, CGRP acts on endothelial cells that line blood vessels, producing pronounced vasodilation.
source: When released from peripheral terminals of sensory neurons, CGRP acts on endothelial cells that line blood vessels, producing pronounced vasodilation (Brain et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: Antibodies that scavenge CGRP reduce the vasodilation that triggers migraine.
source: Recent efforts to develop novel therapeutics in the management of migraine led to the successful development of antibodies that scavenge CGRP, reducing the vasodilation that triggers migraine (Ho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: When released into the superficial dorsal horn from the central branches of sensory neurons, CGRP, along with its co-occurring neuropeptide, substance P, potentiates the glutamatergic excitation of postsynaptic neurons.
source: When released into the superficial dorsal horn from the central branches of sensory neurons, CGRP, along with its co-occurring neuropeptide, substance P, potentiates the glutamatergic excitation of postsynaptic neurons, contributing to injury-provoked central sensitization (Ryu et al., 1988; Woolf and Wiesenfeld-Hallin, 1986).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: CGRP and substance P contribute to injury-provoked central sensitization.
source: When released into the superficial dorsal horn from the central branches of sensory neurons, CGRP, along with its co-occurring neuropeptide, substance P, potentiates the glutamatergic excitation of postsynaptic neurons, contributing to injury-provoked central sensitization (Ryu et al., 1988; Woolf and Wiesenfeld-Hallin, 1986).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Central sensitization contributes to the ongoing pain and profound hypersensitivity characteristic of both inflammatory and neuropathic pains.
source: The latter process, in turn, contributes to the ongoing pain and profound hypersensitivity characteristic of both inflammatory and neuropathic pains.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CGRP receptor signaling in the periphery alleviates incision-induced mechanical and heat hypersensitivity, but not neuropathic pain.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that pharmacological inhibition of CGRP receptor signaling in the periphery alleviates incision-induced mechanical and heat hypersensitivity, but not neuropathic pain, suggesting that primary sensory neuron-derived CGRP differentially influences injury-induced persistent pain (Cowie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Primary sensory neuron-derived CGRP differentially influences injury-induced persistent pain.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that pharmacological inhibition of CGRP receptor signaling in the periphery alleviates incision-induced mechanical and heat hypersensitivity, but not neuropathic pain, suggesting that primary sensory neuron-derived CGRP differentially influences injury-induced persistent pain (Cowie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated with a citation to support it.

claim: Earlier reports used colchicine to enhance somatic CGRP levels and detected small CGRP-positive cells in the dorsal horn.
source: Despite much earlier reports, which used colchicine to enhance somatic CGRP levels (Kruger et al., 1988; Tie-Jun et al., 2001) and a more recent report (McCoy et al., 2012) of small CGRP-positive cells in the dorsal horn of a reporter mouse, the prevailing view is that dorsal horn CGRP derives exclusively from afferents.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: A recent report detected small CGRP-positive cells in the dorsal horn of a reporter mouse.
source: Despite much earlier reports, which used colchicine to enhance somatic CGRP levels (Kruger et al., 1988; Tie-Jun et al., 2001) and a more recent report (McCoy et al., 2012) of small CGRP-positive cells in the dorsal horn of a reporter mouse, the prevailing view is that dorsal horn CGRP derives exclusively from afferents.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The prevailing view is that dorsal horn CGRP derives exclusively from afferents.
source: Despite much earlier reports, which used colchicine to enhance somatic CGRP levels (Kruger et al., 1988; Tie-Jun et al., 2001) and a more recent report (McCoy et al., 2012) of small CGRP-positive cells in the dorsal horn of a reporter mouse, the prevailing view is that dorsal horn CGRP derives exclusively from afferents.
evidence: This is stated as the current scientific consensus in the introduction.

claim: Unlike dorsal horn vertical cells, which have ventrally directed dendrites and a dorsally directed axon, the CGRP interneurons have mainly dorsally directed dendrites and ventrally directed axons.
source: Unlike dorsal horn vertical cells, which have ventrally directed dendrites and a dorsally directed axon, the CGRP interneurons have mainly dorsally directed dendrites and ventrally directed axons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by anatomical data.

claim: CGRP interneurons are minimally responsive to a host of acute, innocuous or noxious mechanical and chemical stimuli.
source: A comprehensive functional analysis showed that these interneurons are minimally responsive to a host of acute, innocuous or noxious mechanical and chemical stimuli, despite the fact that electrical stimulation of Aβ afferents readily activates the cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by Fos expression data.

claim: Electrical stimulation of Aβ afferents readily activates CGRP interneurons.
source: A comprehensive functional analysis showed that these interneurons are minimally responsive to a host of acute, innocuous or noxious mechanical and chemical stimuli, despite the fact that electrical stimulation of Aβ afferents readily activates the cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: An innocuous mechanical stimulus evoked significant Fos expression in CGRP interneurons in the setting of peripheral nerve injury.
source: On the other hand, an innocuous mechanical stimulus evoked significant Fos expression in the setting of peripheral nerve injury and chemogenetic activation of the interneurons produced clear mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by Fos expression data after SNI.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of CGRP interneurons produced clear mechanical hypersensitivity.
source: On the other hand, an innocuous mechanical stimulus evoked significant Fos expression in the setting of peripheral nerve injury and chemogenetic activation of the interneurons produced clear mechanical hypersensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by DREADD activation experiments.

claim: Caspase-mediated ablation of CGRP interneurons increased mechanical thresholds.
source: Conversely, caspase-mediated ablation of the neurons increased mechanical thresholds.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by ablation experiments.

claim: CGRP-expressing interneurons engage deep dorsal horn nociresponsive circuits that contribute either to ascending circuits originating in deep dorsal horn or to the reflex circuits in baseline conditions, but not in the setting of nerve injury.
source: We conclude that these CGRP-expressing interneurons engage deep dorsal horn nociresponsive circuits that contribute either to ascending circuits originating in deep dorsal horn or to the reflex circuits in baseline conditions, but not in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the introduction based on the experimental findings.

claim: 80% of tdTomato-positive neurons in trigeminal ganglia and DRG immunostained for CGRP.
source: Figure 1 illustrates that 80% of tdTomato-positive neurons in trigeminal ganglia (TG) and DRG immunostained for CGRP and that 78% of the CGRP immunoreactive neurons were tdTomato-positive (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 78% of the CGRP immunoreactive neurons in trigeminal ganglia and DRG were tdTomato-positive.
source: Figure 1 illustrates that 80% of tdTomato-positive neurons in trigeminal ganglia (TG) and DRG immunostained for CGRP and that 78% of the CGRP immunoreactive neurons were tdTomato-positive (Figure 1a–d).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The pattern of CGRP-expression observed in the CalcaCreER mouse provides a reliable marker of CGRP-expressing neurons in the adult.
source: We conclude that the pattern of CGRP-expression observed in the CalcaCreER mouse provides a reliable marker of CGRP-expressing neurons in the adult.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the validation data.

claim: Calca mRNA is present in neurons in the spinal cord dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis.
source: However, by in situ hybridization we confirmed that Calca mRNA is present in neurons in the same regions of the spinal cord dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis (Figure 1g–h), which is consistent with the single cell PCR reports of Calca message in subpopulations of dorsal horn neurons (Häring et al., 2018; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 1g-h, with citations to support consistency with prior reports.

claim: Single cell PCR reports detected Calca message in subpopulations of dorsal horn neurons.
source: However, by in situ hybridization we confirmed that Calca mRNA is present in neurons in the same regions of the spinal cord dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis (Figure 1g–h), which is consistent with the single cell PCR reports of Calca message in subpopulations of dorsal horn neurons (Häring et al., 2018; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The lack of CGRP immunostaining in dorsal horn neurons reflects rapid transport of the peptide from the cell body to its axon.
source: We speculate that the lack of CGRP immunostaining reflects rapid transport of the peptide from the cell body to its axon, which undoubtedly underlies the requirement for colchicine to demonstrate these neurons by immunocytochemistry (Kruger et al., 1988; Tie-Jun et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation stated in the results with citations to support the colchicine requirement.

claim: CGRP-positive interneurons are particularly abundant at the most caudal levels of the nucleus caudalis, markedly decreasing rostrally as the hypoglossal nucleus appears.
source: We found the CGRP-positive interneurons to be particularly abundant at the most caudal levels of the nucleus caudalis, markedly decreasing rostrally as the hypoglossal nucleus appears (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: No CGRP-expressing projection neurons were found despite extensive retrograde tracing analysis.
source: Despite an extensive analysis, which included injections into the ventrobasal and nucleus submedius (Yoshida et al., 1991) of the thalamus, lateral parabrachial nucleus (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2b–c for injection site in the parabrachial nucleus), and dorsal column nuclei, which are targeted by postsynaptic dorsal column neurons located in the region of lamina IV of the dorsal horn, we found no evidence of CGRP-expressing projection neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: No long-distance axonal projections deriving from the lamina III CGRP cells were found after anterograde tracing with AAV1-flex-GCaMP6s virus.
source: This finding was confirmed with an anterograde-tracing approach in which we injected an AAV1-flex-GCaMP6s virus unilaterally into the nucleus caudalis of CalcaCreER/tdTomato mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a). After 4 weeks, we examined the brainstem, thalamus, and hypothalamus for GFP-labeled fibers, but found no evidence of long-distance axonal projections deriving from the lamina III CGRP cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on anterograde tracing experiments.

claim: 98% of CGRP-tdTomato cells co-express Lmx1b.
source: First, the CGRP-tdTomato cells co-express Lmx1b (98%; 92/94 tdTomato cells), but not Pax2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which are excitatory and inhibitory markers, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: CGRP-tdTomato cells do not co-express Pax2.
source: First, the CGRP-tdTomato cells co-express Lmx1b (98%; 92/94 tdTomato cells), but not Pax2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which are excitatory and inhibitory markers, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lmx1b is an excitatory marker.
source: First, the CGRP-tdTomato cells co-express Lmx1b (98%; 92/94 tdTomato cells), but not Pax2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which are excitatory and inhibitory markers, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results.

claim: Pax2 is an inhibitory marker.
source: First, the CGRP-tdTomato cells co-express Lmx1b (98%; 92/94 tdTomato cells), but not Pax2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which are excitatory and inhibitory markers, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results.

claim: Approximately 16% of CGRP-tdTomato cells co-expressed PKCγ.
source: Some of the CGRP-tdTomato cells populate inner lamina II, and here approximately 16% co-expressed PKCγ (31/187 tdTomato cells), a marker of a large population of excitatory interneurons (Malmberg et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 2, with a citation to support PKCγ as a marker.

claim: PKCγ is a marker of a large population of excitatory interneurons.
source: Some of the CGRP-tdTomato cells populate inner lamina II, and here approximately 16% co-expressed PKCγ (31/187 tdTomato cells), a marker of a large population of excitatory interneurons (Malmberg et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: 63% of the CGRP interneurons co-expressed calbindin.
source: Sixty-three (97/158 tdTomato cells) and 9% (9/97 tdTomato cells) of the CGRP interneurons co-expressed calbindin and calretinin, respectively, calcium binding proteins that mark subpopulations of excitatory dorsal horn interneurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: 9% of the CGRP interneurons co-expressed calretinin.
source: Sixty-three (97/158 tdTomato cells) and 9% (9/97 tdTomato cells) of the CGRP interneurons co-expressed calbindin and calretinin, respectively, calcium binding proteins that mark subpopulations of excitatory dorsal horn interneurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Calbindin and calretinin are calcium binding proteins that mark subpopulations of excitatory dorsal horn interneurons.
source: Sixty-three (97/158 tdTomato cells) and 9% (9/97 tdTomato cells) of the CGRP interneurons co-expressed calbindin and calretinin, respectively, calcium binding proteins that mark subpopulations of excitatory dorsal horn interneurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results.

claim: The incomplete immunohistochemical overlap with major neurochemical classes of dorsal horn interneurons indicates that the CGRP interneurons are heterogeneous.
source: The incomplete immunohistochemical overlap with major neurochemical classes of dorsal horn interneurons indicates that the CGRP interneurons are heterogeneous consistent with previously described populations of dorsal horn neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the immunohistochemical data.

claim: 56% of Calca-expressing cells express Rora mRNA.
source: Consistent with the concentration of tdTomato-CGRP interneurons in lamina III, particularly notable is that 56% of the Calca mRNA-expressing (CGRP) cells double-labeled for Rora message (639/1134 Calca mRNA-expressing cells), a marker of excitatory interneurons in lamina III (Bourane et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 3, with a citation to support Rora as a marker.

claim: Rora is a marker of excitatory interneurons in lamina III.
source: Consistent with the concentration of tdTomato-CGRP interneurons in lamina III, particularly notable is that 56% of the Calca mRNA-expressing (CGRP) cells double-labeled for Rora message (639/1134 Calca mRNA-expressing cells), a marker of excitatory interneurons in lamina III (Bourane et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Only 4% of Calca-expressing cells co-expressed Cck.
source: Interestingly, however, only 4% co-expressed Cck (27/595 Calca mRNA-expressing cells), which marks a significant subset of the RORα population (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 3, with a citation to support Cck as a marker.

claim: Cck marks a significant subset of the RORα population.
source: Interestingly, however, only 4% co-expressed Cck (27/595 Calca mRNA-expressing cells), which marks a significant subset of the RORα population (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: There is minimal overlap of CGRP interneurons with the population that transiently expresses VGLUT3.
source: As for other populations of excitatory interneurons, we found minimal overlap with the population that transiently expresses VGLUT3 (examined at P7) (Peirs et al., 2015) or others that express Nptx2, BDNF or the NK1 receptor, a marker of many projection neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results with a citation to support VGLUT3 as a marker.

claim: There is minimal overlap of CGRP interneurons with populations that express Nptx2, BDNF or the NK1 receptor.
source: As for other populations of excitatory interneurons, we found minimal overlap with the population that transiently expresses VGLUT3 (examined at P7) (Peirs et al., 2015) or others that express Nptx2, BDNF or the NK1 receptor, a marker of many projection neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results.

claim: The NK1 receptor is a marker of many projection neurons.
source: As for other populations of excitatory interneurons, we found minimal overlap with the population that transiently expresses VGLUT3 (examined at P7) (Peirs et al., 2015) or others that express Nptx2, BDNF or the NK1 receptor, a marker of many projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results.

claim: A substantial portion of the CGRP interneuron population overlaps with a subset of the Cck-negative RORα population of lamina III interneurons.
source: We conclude that a substantial portion of the CGRP interneuron population overlaps with a subset of the Cck-negative RORα population of lamina III interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the in situ hybridization data.

claim: The CGRP interneurons have many dorsally-directed, spine-laden dendrites.
source: Figure 4 illustrates that the CGRP interneurons have many dorsally-directed, spine-laden dendrites.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dendritic arbors of CGRP interneurons often penetrated lamina II, and some labeled processes appeared to reach lamina I.
source: These dendritic arbors often penetrated lamina II, and some labeled processes appeared to reach lamina I.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on anatomical observations.

claim: There is significant synaptic input to the soma, dendrites, and spines of the CGRP interneurons.
source: Furthermore, EM analysis of these interneurons (Figure 5) illustrates that there is significant synaptic input to the soma, dendrites, and spines of the CGRP interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 4c-e.

claim: VGLUT1-immunoreactive axon terminals form many close appositions onto the cell bodies and dendrites of the CGRP interneurons.
source: Indeed when we double-immunostained for tdTomato and VGLUT1, a glutamate transporter that is highly expressed in large myelinated afferents (Oliveira et al., 2003), we observed many close appositions of VGLUT1-immunoreactive axon terminals onto the cell bodies and dendrites of the CGRP interneurons (Figure 4f–j).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 4f-j, with a citation to support VGLUT1 as a marker.

claim: VGLUT1 is a glutamate transporter that is highly expressed in large myelinated afferents.
source: Indeed when we double-immunostained for tdTomato and VGLUT1, a glutamate transporter that is highly expressed in large myelinated afferents (Oliveira et al., 2003), we observed many close appositions of VGLUT1-immunoreactive axon terminals onto the cell bodies and dendrites of the CGRP interneurons (Figure 4f–j).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The CGRP-tdTomato neurons in the dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis showed mostly delayed firing patterns.
source: The CGRP-tdTomato neurons in the dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis showed mostly delayed firing patterns, consistent with their excitatory and radial phenotype (delayed 19, tonic 1, reluctant 2, single 2, no response 3, Figure 6—source data 1 table).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Of five CGRP-tdTomato cells recorded in three mice, all received monosynaptic Aβ input.
source: Of five cells recorded in three mice, all received monosynaptic Aβ input.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The intrinsic properties of neurons recorded from lumbar dorsal horn and nucleus caudalis were comparable.
source: Overall, the intrinsic properties of neurons recorded from lumbar dorsal horn (22 cells, eight mice) and nucleus caudalis (5 cells, two mice) were comparable (see Figure 6—source data 1 table).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The predominant (monosynaptic) input to the CGRP interneurons derives from low threshold (Aβ) mechanoreceptors.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the predominant (monosynaptic) input to the CGRP interneurons derives from low threshold (Aβ) mechanoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Concurrent blocking of the GABA and glycine receptors significantly reduced rheobase in CGRP interneurons.
source: Figure 7a–d illustrate that concurrent blocking of the GABA and glycine receptors significantly reduced rheobase, from 46.0 ± 7.4 pA before antagonist treatment to 31.0 ± 4.9 pA after antagonist treatment (two-tailed, paired T-test; p=0.0005, n = 25).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 7d, with statistical analysis.

claim: Of the 25 neurons studied, rheobase decreased in 21, increased in one and did not change in 3 after blocking GABA and glycine receptors.
source: Of the 25 neurons studied, rheobase decreased in 21, increased in one and did not change in 3.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding stated in the results based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Application of bicuculline and strychnine to neurons in which current was maintained 10 pA below rheobase generated action potentials.
source: Figure 7c shows that application of bicuculline and strychnine to neurons in which current was maintained 10 pA below rheobase also generated action potentials.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Resting membrane potential showed a significant depolarization after application of the GABA and glycine receptor antagonists.
source: Figure 7e shows that resting membrane potential also showed a significant depolarization after application of the GABA and glycine receptor antagonists, from −53.8 ± 1.8 mV before antagonist treatment to −49.1 ± 1.7 mV after antagonist.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The CGRP interneurons, under resting conditions, are under tonic inhibitory control.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the CGRP interneurons, under resting conditions, are under tonic inhibitory control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: A unilateral injection of dilute formalin into the cheek produced considerable Fos immunolabeling of dorsal horn neurons, but not of the CGRP-tdTomato interneurons.
source: As expected, a unilateral injection of dilute formalin into the cheek (10 µl of 2% formalin, Figure 8—figure supplement 1c) or a unilateral hindpaw injection of capsaicin (Figure 8—figure supplement 2a–b), produced considerable Fos immunolabeling of dorsal horn neurons, but not of the CGRP-tdTomato interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplements 1c and 2a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A unilateral hindpaw injection of capsaicin produced considerable Fos immunolabeling of dorsal horn neurons, but not of the CGRP-tdTomato interneurons.
source: As expected, a unilateral injection of dilute formalin into the cheek (10 µl of 2% formalin, Figure 8—figure supplement 1c) or a unilateral hindpaw injection of capsaicin (Figure 8—figure supplement 2a–b), produced considerable Fos immunolabeling of dorsal horn neurons, but not of the CGRP-tdTomato interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplements 1c and 2a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: Selectively engaging non-nociceptive afferents by having the animal walk for 90 min on a rotarod did not induce Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons.
source: Unexpectedly, however, selectively engaging non-nociceptive afferents by having the animal walk for 90 min on a rotarod, which provokes considerable Fos in laminae III and IV (Neumann et al., 2008), did not induce Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a, with a citation to support the Fos induction in laminae III and IV.

claim: Walking on a rotarod provokes considerable Fos in laminae III and IV.
source: Unexpectedly, however, selectively engaging non-nociceptive afferents by having the animal walk for 90 min on a rotarod, which provokes considerable Fos in laminae III and IV (Neumann et al., 2008), did not induce Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Brushing of the cheek did not induce Fos expression in the CGRP interneurons in uninjured mice.
source: The same was true for brushing of the cheek, another innocuous stimulus that activates Aβ afferents (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Systemic injection of nitroglycerin did not induce Fos in the CGRP interneurons.
source: Finally, although CGRP is strongly implicated in the generation of migraine, largely but not exclusively via its peripheral vasodilatory action (Brain et al., 1985), systemic injection of nitroglycerin, which triggers migraine in humans and profound mechanical hypersensitivity in animals (Bates et al., 2010), did not induce Fos in the CGRP interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1b, with citations to support the role of CGRP in migraine and the effects of nitroglycerin.

claim: CGRP is strongly implicated in the generation of migraine, largely but not exclusively via its peripheral vasodilatory action.
source: Finally, although CGRP is strongly implicated in the generation of migraine, largely but not exclusively via its peripheral vasodilatory action (Brain et al., 1985), systemic injection of nitroglycerin, which triggers migraine in humans and profound mechanical hypersensitivity in animals (Bates et al., 2010), did not induce Fos in the CGRP interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Nitroglycerin triggers migraine in humans and profound mechanical hypersensitivity in animals.
source: Finally, although CGRP is strongly implicated in the generation of migraine, largely but not exclusively via its peripheral vasodilatory action (Brain et al., 1985), systemic injection of nitroglycerin, which triggers migraine in humans and profound mechanical hypersensitivity in animals (Bates et al., 2010), did not induce Fos in the CGRP interneurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Despite sufficient input to activate CGRP interneurons under natural innocuous mechanical stimulus conditions in uninjured mice, there does not appear to be sufficient input to activate these cells (5.3%, 5/88 tdTomato cells).
source: We conclude that despite our electrophysiological evidence that Aβ afferents engage the CGRP interneurons, there does not appear to be sufficient input to activate these cells under natural innocuous mechanical stimulus conditions in uninjured mice (5.3%, 5/88 tdTomato cells; Figure 8a).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the Fos expression data.

claim: Six days after inducing the spared nerve injury (SNI) model of neuropathic pain, brushing the ipsilateral paw evoked Fos expression in 50% (53/110 tdTomato cells) of the dorsal horn CGRP interneurons.
source: In fact six days after inducing the spared nerve injury (SNI) model of neuropathic pain, we found that brushing the ipsilateral paw evoked Fos expression in 50% (53/110 tdTomato cells) of the dorsal horn CGRP interneurons (Figure 8c and d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8c and d.

claim: Significant dorsal horn Fos expression occurred in nerve-injured mice without brushing, but no Fos expression occurred in the CGRP interneurons (3%; 6/205 tdTomato cells).
source: Importantly, although we recorded significant dorsal horn Fos expression in nerve-injured mice without brushing (Figure 8b), no Fos expression occurred in the CGRP interneurons (3%; 6/205 tdTomato cells).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Activation of the CGRP interneurons only occurs when the innocuous input engages the interneurons in the setting of nerve injury.
source: We conclude that activation of the CGRP interneurons only occurs when the innocuous input, which could include contact of the plantar surface of the paw with the ground (Liu et al., 2018), engages the interneurons in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the Fos expression data, with a citation to support the type of innocuous input.

claim: CNO injection in the DREADD-expressing group produced a significant reduction of von Frey threshold of the ipsilateral hindpaw, compared to baseline or to saline-injected mice.
source: Figure 9 shows that CNO injection in the experimental group produced a significant reduction of von Frey threshold of the ipsilateral hindpaw, compared to baseline or to saline-injected mice (Figure 9b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 9b, with statistical analysis.

claim: Mechanical thresholds did not change from baseline in the AAV-GFP control animals, whether they received saline or CNO.
source: Mechanical thresholds did not change from baseline in the AAV-GFP control animals, whether they received saline or CNO (Repeated Measures Two-way ANOVA, F(1,20)=6.964, p=0.012, interaction effect between DREADD group and CNO treatment).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results with statistical analysis.

claim: Mice in which CGRP-expressing spinal cord interneurons were ablated with a virally derived caspase exhibited significantly higher mechanical thresholds than did control mice.
source: Consistent with a contribution of CGRP-expressing interneurons to mechanical sensitivity, mice in which we ablated selectively the CGRP-expressing spinal cord interneurons with a virally derived caspase (Figure 10a and Figure 10—figure supplement 1) exhibited significantly higher mechanical thresholds than did control mice (Figure 10b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 10b.

claim: The mechanical hypersensitivity produced in the SNI model of neuropathic pain was not altered by the ablation of CGRP interneurons.
source: On the other hand, and somewhat unexpectedly, the mechanical hypersensitivity produced in the SNI model of neuropathic pain was not altered by the ablation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results.

claim: Neither latency to withdraw the hindpaw to noxious heat in the Hargreaves test nor time spent paw lifting after exposure of the plantar surface of the hindpaw to a cold (acetone) stimulus differed when comparing CNO and control saline injection.
source: Lastly, we evaluated heat and cold responsiveness after CNO injection. Neither latency to withdraw the hindpaw to noxious heat in the Hargreaves test (n = 16; Figure 9d) nor time spent paw lifting after exposure of the plantar surface of the hindpaw to a cold (acetone) stimulus (n = 11; Figure 9e), differed when comparing CNO and control saline injection (p>0.05, Students T-test and Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 9d-e, with statistical analysis.

claim: Responses to noxious heat (Hargreaves) or cold (acetone) stimuli were unchanged after caspase-mediated ablation of the CGRP-expressing interneurons.
source: Similarly, responses to noxious heat (Hargreaves; Figure 10c) or cold (acetone; Figure 10d) stimuli were unchanged after caspase-mediated ablation of the CGRP-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 10c-d.

claim: Direct and likely synchronous activation of the CGRP interneurons produces a selective mechanical hypersensitivity, mimicking the mechanical allodynia observed in response to low threshold (Aβ) mechanical stimulation (brush) in the setting of nerve injury.
source: We conclude that direct and likely synchronous activation of the CGRP interneurons produces a selective mechanical hypersensitivity, mimicking the mechanical allodynia observed in response to low threshold (Aβ) mechanical stimulation (brush) in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the DREADD and ablation experiments.

claim: Several populations of dorsal horn excitatory neurons that express Calca mRNA co-express gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP).
source: Based on their single cell transcriptome analysis, Häring and colleagues (Häring et al., 2018) concluded that several populations of dorsal horn excitatory neurons that express Calca mRNA co-express gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), a peptide linked to dorsal horn circuits that drive itch-provoked scratching (Albisetti et al., 2019; Sun and Chen, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: GRP is a peptide linked to dorsal horn circuits that drive itch-provoked scratching.
source: Based on their single cell transcriptome analysis, Häring and colleagues (Häring et al., 2018) concluded that several populations of dorsal horn excitatory neurons that express Calca mRNA co-express gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), a peptide linked to dorsal horn circuits that drive itch-provoked scratching (Albisetti et al., 2019; Sun and Chen, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Double in situ hybridization found several instances of co-localization of Calca mRNA and Grp mRNA.
source: To confirm this, we performed double in situ hybridization for Calca and Grp. Although the Grp interneurons predominated in a band just dorsal to the Calca interneurons, consistent with our previous report (Solorzano et al., 2015), we did find several instances of co-localization of Calca mRNA and Grp mRNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results with a citation to support the distribution of Grp interneurons.

claim: Using immunohistochemistry, there was almost no overlap of GRP and CGRP in a double transgenic GRP-GFP/CGRP-tdTomato mouse line.
source: Interestingly, however, when using immunohistochemistry, we found almost no overlap of GRP and CGRP in a double transgenic GRP-GFP/CGRP-tdTomato mouse line (Figure 11a–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 11c-d.

claim: Neurons labeled in the GRP-GFP reporter mouse constitute less than half of the Grp mRNA-positive population.
source: This difference is likely related to the fact that neurons labeled in the reporter mouse constitute less than half of the Grp mRNA-positive population (Solorzano et al., 2015; Dickie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Despite considerable chloroquine-induced Fos expression, only an occasional double-labeled neuron was found.
source: As Figure 11e–f illustrates, despite considerable chloroquine-induced Fos expression, we found only an occasional double-labeled neuron.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 11e-f.

claim: The number of scratching bouts induced by a subcutaneous calf injection of 100 μg chloroquine was comparable between control and CGRP-ablated mice.
source: Furthermore, the number of scratching bouts induced by a subcutaneous calf injection of 100 μg chloroquine was comparable between control and CGRP-ablated mice (Figure 10e).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and shown in Figure 10e.

claim: The CGRP interneurons, despite some overlap with GRP, likely do not transmit chemical itch.
source: We conclude that the CGRP interneurons, despite some overlap with GRP, likely do not transmit chemical itch, a finding consistent with the effects of deleting RORα (Bourane et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the itch experiments, with a citation to support consistency with RORα deletion.

claim: Deletion of RORα does not affect chemical itch.
source: We conclude that the CGRP interneurons, despite some overlap with GRP, likely do not transmit chemical itch, a finding consistent with the effects of deleting RORα (Bourane et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is implied by the statement that the finding is consistent with the effects of deleting RORα, with a citation to support it.

claim: The dorsal horn CGRP interneurons represent the first class of excitatory interneurons in lamina III that are unresponsive to innocuous mechanical stimulation under basal conditions despite receiving a monosynaptic Aβ input.
source: To our knowledge, the CGRP interneurons represent the first class of excitatory interneurons in lamina III that are unresponsive to innocuous mechanical stimulation under basal conditions despite receiving a monosynaptic Aβ input.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Reduction of inhibitory inputs in the setting of injury would render the CGRP neurons responsive to an innocuous stimulus.
source: One possibility is that the CGRP interneurons are tonically inhibited under normal conditions, which is consistent with our electrophysiological recordings showing bicuculline-mediated facilitation of these interneurons. Reduction of these inhibitory inputs in the setting of injury (Torsney and MacDermott, 2006) would render the neurons responsive to an innocuous stimulus (e.g. brush).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion with a citation to support the reduction of inhibitory inputs after injury.

claim: The ventrally directed axons of CGRP interneurons could drive reflex withdrawal circuits and/or engage ascending nociceptive pathways located in deep dorsal horn.
source: In turn, the ventrally directed axons of these interneurons could drive reflex withdrawal circuits, which is consistent with increased mechanical thresholds in the CGRP-interneuron ablated mice, and/or engage ascending nociceptive pathways located in deep dorsal horn.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion based on the anatomical and functional data.

claim: Sensitization of CGRP interneurons is critical to mechanisms that underlie Aβ-mediated mechanical allodynia in the setting of nerve injury.
source: The fact that DREADD-mediated direct activation of many CGRP interneurons lowered mechanical withdrawal thresholds is consistent with that hypothesis. In other words, we suggest that sensitization of these neurons is critical to mechanisms that underlie Aβ-mediated mechanical allodynia in the setting of nerve injury.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion based on the DREADD experiments.

claim: Lu et al., 2013 provided evidence for convergence of a primary afferent-derived Aβ and a tonic glycinergic inhibitory input to PKCγ interneurons.
source: Interestingly, Lu et al., 2013 provided evidence for convergence of a primary afferent-derived Aβ and a tonic glycinergic inhibitory input to PKCγ interneurons, some of which we found express CGRP.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Loss of glycinergic inhibition allowed Aβ input to access lamina I nociceptive circuits.
source: Loss of this glycinergic inhibition allowed Aβ input to access lamina I nociceptive circuits.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited study.

claim: Other studies demonstrated a comparable outcome by a presynaptic glycinergic inhibition of non-nociceptive inputs to superficial dorsal horn neurons.
source: Other studies demonstrated a comparable outcome, in this case by a presynaptic glycinergic inhibition of non-nociceptive inputs to superficial dorsal horn neurons (Sherman and Loomis, 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Imlach et al., 2016 proposed that decreased glycinergic inhibition is selective for radial cells in lamina II and likely contributes to neuropathic pain.
source: Furthermore, Imlach et al., 2016 proposed that decreased glycinergic inhibition is selective for radial cells in lamina II and likely contributes to neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A comparable circuit involving the CGRP radial cells could uncover low threshold inputs to ventrally located nociceptive circuits.
source: We suggest that a comparable circuit involving the CGRP radial cells could uncover low threshold inputs to ventrally located nociceptive circuits, which in recent years have been largely ignored (Wercberger and Basbaum, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion with a citation to support the notion that ventral circuits have been ignored.
